title: Confucius' one word
hook: Confucius' one word for life: what you don't want done to you, don't do to others (Analects 15.23)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Theravada, and a practice that asks and gives forgiveness in the same breath. Your line was I ask, I forgive.

A student wants it short. Zigong, one of Confucius' disciples, written Tsze-kung in James Legge's old translation, asks his teacher whether there is one word that could serve as a rule of practice for all of a person's life. Not a book, not a list of duties. Something you could carry in your pocket. Confucius doesn't tell him the question is too simple. He gives him the word, and then says what it means.
screen: `ONE WORD FOR A WHOLE LIFE?` → `ZIGONG ASKS.` → `CONFUCIUS ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Confucius answers: shu. Legge translates it reciprocity. Others render it consideration, or putting yourself in another's place. Then he spells it out, in Legge's words: "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." It's phrased as a don't. It doesn't tell you to press on others whatever you happen to like. It starts from what hurts, and asks you not to hand that on. Elsewhere in the Analects, in book four, the disciple Zengzi sums up the Master's whole way in two words, loyalty and shu, and says there's nothing more to it. The word Zigong was given is half of that summary. Why is it here, in a stretch about forgiveness? Shu asks for one move: stand where the other person stood. Forgiveness keeps asking for the same move. Before judging what someone did, you ask what you'd want if you had done it, and what you'd not want done to you. Look back at this week. A verse said idfa': push back harm with better. The Gita listed kshama among the divine qualities. Kabir named it khima: where forgiveness is, there is God himself. Angulimala stopped. The Buddha left an insult with its owner. A chant asked and gave forgiveness together. And now a single word from China, for standing in someone else's shoes.
screen: `ONE WORD: SHU.` · `WHAT YOU DO NOT WANT DONE TO YOURSELF.` · `LOYALTY AND SHU.` · `STANDING WHERE THEY STOOD.` · then, large: `SHU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose actions you've been judging lately, and step, in your mind, into where they were standing: their tiredness, their pressure, what they could see and couldn't. Ask quietly what you'd want from the people around you if you had done this, and what you'd not want done to you, and let your judgment stand next to that question for a while; you don't have to change it.
Shu. Reciprocity, consideration: Confucius' one word, spelled out as what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others. Today's word.
Your line: stand where they stood. One word, carried for a whole life. Day nine hundred sixty-six, done.

howItsDone: Students of Confucius learn the Analects' answer to Zigong as a rule of life, and shu, reciprocity or consideration, is taught alongside zhong, loyalty, as a core of the Master's way.

options: Close, but it's phrased as a don't: what you don't want done to you, don't do to others.
Yes: it says treat others well, and they're sure to treat you well back.
No, it's about loyalty to your ruler, not about how you treat other people.
